tarot-sun.title: The Sun: brightness with perspective
opening: Upright, in a sentence: Acknowledge real progress openly. Show what you have made, and let yourself enjoy it.
Reversed, in a sentence: Is joy hard to feel, or is enthusiasm running ahead of judgment? First work out which difficulty you are facing.

Imagine moving a model you have spent a long time making beside a window: the colours brighten, and the joins become easier to see. The Sun has that kind of honest brightness. It lifts your spirits while making inspection easier.
This article focuses on XIX, the Sun, in the Rider–Waite–Smith (RWS) tradition. We begin with the image and distinguish Waite's traditional interpretation from the modern applications offered here.

sections.title: First, notice who has stepped into the light
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Before memorising “success”, look from the sun overhead down to the child in front of the wall. The picture makes vitality outward and expressive without erasing every boundary.

**The sun and sunflowers: where the light falls.** The enormous sun has a human face, with alternating straight and wavy rays; sunflowers rise behind the wall. The sun fills the sky, while the flowers bring our gaze back to earth. One modern association follows: an abstract sense of “I feel good” is more useful when connected to visible progress, such as a concept you can finally explain clearly. The flowers' number and direction deserve attention, but need not be forced into a single secret code.

**The child and white horse: how strength is used.** The unclothed child sits on a white horse with arms outstretched; no reins are visible. The pairing combines a child's openness with a large animal's strength. Waite discusses simplicity and innocence through the child, as well as the harmony of renewed consciousness with animal nature. Following the image, we might read a confidence that does not require constant tension: having the capacity to support action makes it easier to let go. Openness in real life still requires judgment about whom to trust and where to draw boundaries.

**The wall and red banner: how to express yourself after stepping out.** A grey wall runs behind the figure, who is in front of it; a large red banner unfurls upwards. The wall gives “coming out” a location, and the banner gives joy a gesture. One reading is to let an achievement be seen while acknowledging its limits. You can say, “This step worked,” without declaring the whole future a success. The conspicuous banner also invites a check: when expressing yourself, are you leaving room for others?

sections.title: The traditional Sun goes deeper than a good mood
sections.bodyMarkdown:
In Part Two of *The Pictorial Key to the Tarot*, Waite associates the Sun with the direct light of spiritual consciousness and uses the child to describe innocence accompanied by wisdom. This is his mystical interpretation, not an established psychological mechanism. [Read the English text](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_2)

The divinatory meanings in Part Three are shorter: upright, they concern material happiness, a happy marriage and contentment; reversed, similar meanings remain, but to a lesser degree. The passage is helpful because it reminds beginners that turning a card upside down need not turn its entire meaning into its opposite. [Check the upright and reversed meanings](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3)

sources.label: Read the English text
Check the upright and reversed meanings

sections.title: Ask why, whether upright or reversed
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The upright Sun can help us consider three situations: information is becoming clearer, action is receiving positive feedback, or happiness can be acknowledged without embarrassment. Follow that with, “What fact supports this judgment?” In a relationship, someone stating their intentions matters more than your sense that the atmosphere is pleasant; in studying, explaining a problem independently is more reliable than feeling you understood everything during a lesson.

For a reversal, try two possible readings. These are modern applications, not translations of Waite's wording.

- **The light is difficult to take in.** There is real progress, but you habitually discount yourself; or things are going well and you are already exhausted. Start by making fewer comparisons, acknowledging one small achievement and allowing your feelings time to catch up.
- **The light is too dazzling.** You want only praise, confuse enthusiasm with completion, and treat anyone who mentions a difficulty as a spoilsport. Ask someone willing to be honest to examine the details.

To distinguish them, listen to the person's experience and look at actual feedback. Clear good news that someone struggles to believe fits the first possibility more closely; repeated criticism dismissed out of hand makes the second worth considering. With insufficient evidence, keeping both possibilities open is more honest than rushing towards either a frightening or a pleasing answer.

sections.title: A different deck shifts the emphasis
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The RWS child on horseback readily draws attention to personal openness and the coordination of strength. When comparing other versions, first examine the relationships between figures, then decide how to adjust your interpretation.

Marseille-style Suns often show two figures approaching one another, with a wall behind them. Here you might ask, “Does the light reach both people?” Reading mutual help and shared growth from this is a question this article brings to the image, not a universal conclusion for every Marseille deck. Part One of Waite's book also records the motif of twins and an enclosure in older Sun designs. [An English account of the traditional design](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_1)

The Visconti-Sforza Sun held by the Morgan Library instead shows an unclothed, winged youth on clouds, holding up a radiant human face with both hands. The RWS white horse and sunflowers are absent, so explanations of those six details cannot be imported wholesale. The collection record assigns this card to a later group; it cannot represent every early Italian Sun card either. [Read the collection's description of the object](https://ica.themorgan.org/manuscript/page/13/158525)

The same approach works for modern redesigns: identify what has been added or removed, then ask where those changes direct your attention. If only the sun remains while the people, animals and setting change, observe those relationships afresh. An identical card name does not make every detail's interpretation transferable.

sections.title: A complete worked reading
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**An original fictional example.** Xiaolan is preparing for a portfolio review. She asks, “How should I present this set of work?” The upright Sun appears in the advice position.

First establish the question: she is asking about presentation. The Sun's open posture can inspire her to make the work easier to understand, but cannot establish that she will be selected.

Then connect the picture to facts. Xiaolan has two well-developed pieces, yet keeps introducing them with “It's really nothing special.” The child's ease and the banner's expressiveness can become practical advice: lead with the work that best demonstrates her ability and explain what she did through concrete details of the process.

Next check excessive optimism. The third piece still has unfinished details. Here the wall's sense of a boundary becomes a reminder to distinguish finished work from ongoing experiments when presenting, so confidence does not conceal gaps.

Finally choose an action. Ask a friend to listen to a three-minute introduction, then repeat back “what problem the work solves”. If their account misses the point, adjust the explanation. The Sun's brightness becomes clarity that can be checked.

If the card were reversed in the same position, first ask about her difficulty. If she has received good feedback but fears showing the work, begin with a small practice audience; if she thinks preparation is unnecessary, a candid mock review would be more useful. The same reversed card can lead to actions in two different directions.

sections.title: Leave with one question
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Choose one thing that makes you happy today, write down the evidence for it, and add, “What do I still need to see clearly?” This lets joy stand while leaving room for the next step.

Tarot can help organise thoughts; questions about health or pregnancy should be addressed through examinations and professional advice. Real outcomes still need to be judged using actual information.

why-the-four-fours-differ.title: Why the four Fours read differently
opening: All are Fours, yet one raises flowers, one folds their arms, one lies still and one grips tightly. The differences lie in how the figures relate to the world around them.

Lay the RWS Four of Wands, Four of Cups, Four of Swords and Four of Pentacles side by side, without opening a book of meanings. Ask just three questions: Who can move? Where are the objects? Is there a way between the person and the outside world? This group is a useful exercise in testing abstract ideas against images.

Modern interpretations often treat “four” as stability, structure or boundaries. This is a framework of numerical symbolism, not a natural law shared by every deck. Even if we provisionally use that framework, we still need to ask: what has become stable, and at what cost? The comparison below centres on RWS imagery and offers one way of reading, rather than a single answer for all four cards.

sections.title: Start with hands and feet
sections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Four of Wands, four staffs stand in the foreground with a garland strung between them, while figures behind raise bouquets. The staffs do not weigh down their bodies, and nobody needs to clutch them to keep the structure standing. Waite associates the card with peace, harmony and the repose of a home. [The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Wands](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktwa04.htm)

This supports a possible interpretation: an arrangement has become reliable enough for people to give their attention to shared life. In a team, it might prompt you to examine whether the division of work is functioning and whether a milestone deserves collective recognition. There is no marriage certificate in the picture, so declaring a wedding merely because you see a garland goes beyond what the image supports.

The Four of Pentacles offers a contrast: the figure holds one pentacle against the chest, presses one beneath each foot, and has another above the head. Waite's description emphasises holding on to what one has. [The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Pentacles](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe04.htm)

Stability here requires the body's continuous involvement. Try imagining that posture: with your arms and feet occupied, how much freedom remains to receive something new? This supports a reading in which protecting resources can reduce flexibility, but one card cannot establish that someone is miserly. Caution on a tight budget and unwillingness to cooperate despite having ample resources may look similar while arising from different circumstances.

sources.label: The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Wands
The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Pentacles

sections.title: Two kinds of stillness
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The figure in the Four of Cups sits under a tree, with three cups in front and another offered by a hand extending from a cloud. He does not reach to take it. Waite writes of dissatisfaction with one's surroundings and weariness after satisfaction. [The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Cups](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)

The key question is not whether there are enough things, but whether something new can enter one's attention. For reflection, ask: do I really not need this option, or has fatigue temporarily drained my interest in everything? The two answers call for different next steps; “missing an opportunity” cannot decide between them in advance.

The Four of Swords places stillness in a different setting. Waite explicitly identifies the central figure as a knight's tomb effigy in a posture of prayer; it should not simply be treated as a living person asleep. His interpretations include retreat, solitude and rest. [The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Swords](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktsw04.htm)

Modern readers often use this to discuss pausing, recovery or delaying a response. That is a practical application of a still image, not a diagnosis or prediction of death from a card. Compared with the Four of Cups, a useful question is: am I reducing stimulation so that I can think again, or am I shutting out every suggestion? A single card cannot identify your motive for you, but it can help make the question more specific.

sources.label: The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Cups
The Pictorial Key to the Tarot: Four of Swords

sections.title: Four prompts for the same situation
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Suppose the reading group you run with friends has reached its third month, and you are deciding whether to expand. This is an original exercise, not a record of an actual draw.

- Four of Wands: Keep the processes that already work, and let members share what they have achieved. Stability comes from arrangements everyone can use together.
- Four of Cups: Find out why engagement is falling first. Adding activities may not resolve fatigue; it may simply offer another cup.
- Four of Swords: Allow the organisers time to review and take a break from the schedule. A short pause can have clear limits and a return date.
- Four of Pentacles: Check who controls the budget and decision-making authority. Reserves have value, but one person holding every decision may also impede cooperation.

None of these cards is inherently “best”. What matters is whether stability at this stage gives people spare capacity or makes movement difficult.

sections.title: A new deck calls for new questions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
When comparing decks, first inspect what the particular version actually shows. Early pip cards often indicate their number through repeated suit signs, without the human scenes found in RWS. The posture of refusal beneath a tree cannot simply be transferred to every Four of Cups. [The Metropolitan Museum of Art: tarot's history and structure](https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/tarot-2)

Interpretive traditions also disagree. In his 1888 booklet, for example, Mathers lists the Four of Pentacles in terms of pleasure and contentment, unlike Waite's emphasis on possession. The modern editor of that text specifically cautions that this early work should not be equated with the Golden Dawn's later internal system of correspondences. [Mathers: The Tarot and the editorial note](https://hermeticgoldendawn.org/the-tarot/)

The value of comparison is therefore not finding an eternally correct dictionary. It is learning to explain which images and tradition you are using, and how you move from an image to an interpretation.

sources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: tarot's history and structure
Mathers: The Tarot and the editorial note

sections.title: A five-minute exercise
sections.bodyMarkdown: Choose the four Fours. Write one action word for each, then “what this action protects” and “what it restricts”. For the same real-life question, propose one practical action for each card. Finally remove any assertion for which you can identify neither a visual basis nor a way to check it in real life. Explaining where an interpretation comes from is more useful than memorising more keywords.

how-to-connect-three-tarot-cards.title: How to connect three tarot cards
opening: To turn three separate meanings into an answer people can discuss, focus on the relationships between the cards.

If you draw the Eight of Pentacles, Four of Cups and Three of Pentacles and say only “effort, boredom, cooperation”, you have not yet answered the question. Keywords are like three tools laid on a table: a reading still needs to explain which is operating, which presents an obstacle, and which might change the situation.

The following original exercise uses RWS imagery to demonstrate that process. It is a method of reflection and storytelling, without guaranteed predictions, and cannot replace checking real-world evidence.

sections.title: Decide what the three cards are answering first
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Imagine a designer asking, “I keep revising my portfolio. How can I make my next round of job preparation more effective?” Before turning the cards, she assigns three positions: what I am putting effort into, where I may get stuck, and what I can try next.

This sets limits on interpretation. The Four of Cups in an “obstacle” position might raise questions about attention and engagement; in an “available resource” position it might invite discussion of careful selection or delaying acceptance. A position changes the angle of the question, but does not allow any card to mean anything at will.

Nor should “situation, obstacle, advice” suddenly become “past, present, future” after you see the cards. That makes the interpretation easier to justify to itself and harder to examine. Write down the question and positions before practising, and keep them as written.

sections.title: Describe the image before interpreting it
sections.bodyMarkdown:
First, the Eight of Pentacles: a craftsperson is making pentacles, with completed pieces neatly displayed. Waite's text associates it with work, skill and preparation. For now, note “continuing to refine a specific piece of work”. [Waite: Eight of Pentacles](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe08.htm)

Second, the Four of Cups: a seated figure has three cups in front, and another is being offered, but he does not reach to receive it. Note “something is offered from outside; a response has not yet occurred”. “Boredom” is already an interpretation; not taking the cup is the visual evidence we can discuss. [Waite: Four of Cups](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)

Third, the Three of Pentacles: a craftsperson works within a building, with two other people nearby, one holding a plan. Waite emphasises skilled work and explicitly asks the reader to compare it with the Eight of Pentacles. “Bring the work into a shared discussion” develops a reading from the picture; it is not a word-for-word definition in his text. [Waite: Three of Pentacles](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe03.htm)

This distinction matters: separating “I can see” from “I infer” lets a reader identify which steps are well supported and which need more information.

sources.label: Waite: Eight of Pentacles
Waite: Four of Cups
Waite: Three of Pentacles

sections.title: Add a connecting word between neighbouring cards
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Modern tarot teaching includes a technique called bridging: making visual or intuitive connections between symbols within the question's context. It is an interpretive exercise, not a validated mechanism of prediction. [Barbara Moore: Practical Techniques for Better Readings](https://www.llewellyn.com/blog/2019/09/practical-techniques-for-better-readings/)

In this example, look first only at the Eight of Pentacles and Four of Cups. One person keeps working; the other does not receive what is offered. Place “but” between them: “You keep refining the work, but may have become reluctant to take in fresh feedback.”

Then compare the Four of Cups and Three of Pentacles. In one picture a person keeps a distance from what is offered; in the other, several people gather around work. Connect them with “by”: “By inviting others into the discussion, examine whether you are rejecting unhelpful advice or any advice that would change the existing work.”

Finally combine this into one answer: “Pause a round of solitary polishing, discuss the work with someone who can explain the standards it needs to meet, then decide what to change next.” The advice has a visual basis, but “you are rejecting feedback” remains a hypothesis to check.

sources.label: Barbara Moore: Practical Techniques for Better Readings

sections.title: Use counterexamples to keep the story open to correction
sections.bodyMarkdown:
If the designer replies, “I ask three people to look every week; their advice just conflicts,” the interpretation needs to change. You cannot insist that she unconsciously rejects feedback anyway, making the cards right whatever she says.

# How to connect three tarot cards

To turn three separate meanings into an answer people can discuss, focus on the relationships between the cards.

If you draw the Eight of Pentacles, Four of Cups and Three of Pentacles and say only “effort, boredom, cooperation”, you have not yet answered the question. Keywords are like three tools laid on a table: a reading still needs to explain which is operating, which presents an obstacle, and which might change the situation.

The following original exercise uses RWS imagery to demonstrate that process. It is a method of reflection and storytelling, without guaranteed predictions, and cannot replace checking real-world evidence.

## Decide what the three cards are answering first

Imagine a designer asking, “I keep revising my portfolio. How can I make my next round of job preparation more effective?” Before turning the cards, she assigns three positions: what I am putting effort into, where I may get stuck, and what I can try next.

This sets limits on interpretation. The Four of Cups in an “obstacle” position might raise questions about attention and engagement; in an “available resource” position it might invite discussion of careful selection or delaying acceptance. A position changes the angle of the question, but does not allow any card to mean anything at will.

Nor should “situation, obstacle, advice” suddenly become “past, present, future” after you see the cards. That makes the interpretation easier to justify to itself and harder to examine. Write down the question and positions before practising, and keep them as written.

## Describe the image before interpreting it

First, the Eight of Pentacles: a craftsperson is making pentacles, with completed pieces neatly displayed. Waite's text associates it with work, skill and preparation. For now, note “continuing to refine a specific piece of work”. [Waite: Eight of Pentacles](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe08.htm)

Second, the Four of Cups: a seated figure has three cups in front, and another is being offered, but he does not reach to receive it. Note “something is offered from outside; a response has not yet occurred”. “Boredom” is already an interpretation; not taking the cup is the visual evidence we can discuss. [Waite: Four of Cups](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)

Third, the Three of Pentacles: a craftsperson works within a building, with two other people nearby, one holding a plan. Waite emphasises skilled work and explicitly asks the reader to compare it with the Eight of Pentacles. “Bring the work into a shared discussion” develops a reading from the picture; it is not a word-for-word definition in his text. [Waite: Three of Pentacles](https://sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe03.htm)

This distinction matters: separating “I can see” from “I infer” lets a reader identify which steps are well supported and which need more information.

## Add a connecting word between neighbouring cards

Modern tarot teaching includes a technique called bridging: making visual or intuitive connections between symbols within the question's context. It is an interpretive exercise, not a validated mechanism of prediction. [Barbara Moore: Practical Techniques for Better Readings](https://www.llewellyn.com/blog/2019/09/practical-techniques-for-better-readings/)

In this example, look first only at the Eight of Pentacles and Four of Cups. One person keeps working; the other does not receive what is offered. Place “but” between them: “You keep refining the work, but may have become reluctant to take in fresh feedback.”

Then compare the Four of Cups and Three of Pentacles. In one picture a person keeps a distance from what is offered; in the other, several people gather around work. Connect them with “by”: “By inviting others into the discussion, examine whether you are rejecting unhelpful advice or any advice that would change the existing work.”

Finally combine this into one answer: “Pause a round of solitary polishing, discuss the work with someone who can explain the standards it needs to meet, then decide what to change next.” The advice has a visual basis, but “you are rejecting feedback” remains a hypothesis to check.

## Use counterexamples to keep the story open to correction

If the designer replies, “I ask three people to look every week; their advice just conflicts,” the interpretation needs to change. You cannot insist that she unconsciously rejects feedback anyway, making the cards right whatever she says.

A version that fits the information better is: repeated revisions are draining you; too much advice is difficult to absorb; next you need a shared evaluation standard rather than more reviewers. The plan in the Three of Pentacles can now serve as a visual prompt for grounding discussion in shared requirements. A pictured plan does not inherently mean hiring criteria. The connection comes from this question, and we should say so.

Only comparison with the target role, the actual work and previous feedback can show which version is more useful. If real information supports neither, acknowledge that the association has not offered anything useful this time.

## Turn one interpretation into one action

Set a small experiment for this exercise: choose one target role and someone familiar with it. Ask them to look at just one portfolio project and identify the decision process they find hardest to understand. Record the feedback, then make one clearly bounded revision.

A week later, check whether the changes were more focused and whether the other person can explain more quickly what problem the project solves. These are observable changes. They cannot prove the cards foresaw the future, but they can help you judge whether the reading led to clear action.

## Try it yourself

Choose any three cards, first assigning positions for a specific, low-risk question. Write one non-judgmental description of each image, then connect adjacent cards with “but”, “therefore” or “by”. Once you have a one-sentence answer, write an alternative interpretation that fits the images equally well and say what real information would make you choose it instead.

Finish with just one action the person can take. If the answer still amounts to “the universe will arrange it” or “they will definitely come back”, return to the question, positions and images and connect them again. A coherent reading allows others to follow your reasoning and challenge its assumptions.

opening: One of tarot's most interesting historical questions is how people kept finding new uses for the same kind of playing cards.

Look at a gilded fifteenth-century card, then at an RWS card. We may recognise familiar figures, but that does not establish that users separated by centuries were doing the same thing. When discussing tarot history, distinguish three layers: the surviving objects, the interpretations people later gave them, and the stories told about their origins.

sections.title: The earliest reliable clues are at the gaming table
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art places early records of tarot in northern Italy in the mid-fifteenth century. Its structure added a series of trumps and the Fool to four suits, for a trick-taking game: players follow rules for playing cards and try to win a trick. Familiar occult uses form a layer of interpretation that developed widely only centuries later. [The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Before Fortune-Telling](https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/tarot-2)

Rather than a simple claim about “who invented it first”, the precise identity of an object deserves attention. The date, place of production, materials, family emblems and collection history of the Visconti-Sforza cards, for instance, locate them in a real social setting. The Morgan's collection record studies the cards as Renaissance works of art and clearly distinguishes their dating from later claims of Egyptian origins. [The Morgan: Visconti-Sforza collection record](https://www.themorgan.org/manuscript/158525)

The presence of a pope, a virtue or Death on a card shows the use of recognisable imagery of its time. It does not establish that players treated the cards as a secret religious textbook. An image having symbolic meaning and an image being used for divination are two claims that require separate evidence.

sources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Before Fortune-Telling
The Morgan: Visconti-Sforza collection record

sections.title: New origin stories emerged in the eighteenth century
sections.bodyMarkdown:
In 1781, Court de Gébelin interpreted tarot as a remnant of ancient Egyptian wisdom in volume eight of *Le Monde primitif*. De Mellet's essay, immediately following in the same volume, connected it with the Book of Thoth and discussed ways of reading the cards. The Morgan's curatorial account describes this stage as a reshaping of tarot's identity, not the eventual confirmation of an Egyptian origin. [The Morgan: Occult Tarot](https://www.themorgan.org/exhibitions/online/tarot/11)

The distinction is subtle: an origin story can have genuine cultural effects even when it lacks historical evidence. People subsequently wrote books, redesigned cards and established courses on that basis; those activities are themselves part of history. We need to distinguish “someone believed tarot came from Egypt” from “tarot did come from Egypt”. Publications can establish the first; the second requires earlier objects and evidence of transmission.

Alongside these theories, Etteilla, whose name was Jean-Baptiste Alliette, helped teach and spread cartomancy. His works offered diagrams and practical methods. MIT's playing-card research page also notes scattered evidence of divination before extensive publication, so 1781 should not be treated as the year all card divination suddenly began. [MIT: A Brief History of Cartomancy](https://frenchplayingcards.mit.edu/tarot/tarot-history)

sources.label: The Morgan: Occult Tarot
MIT: A Brief History of Cartomancy

sections.title: How occult systems entered the cards
sections.bodyMarkdown:
In the nineteenth century, tarot became increasingly involved in networks of Western occult interpretation. In the setting of the Golden Dawn, studying cards could also involve ritual and correspondences. The V&A places the meeting of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith within that group; their RWS collaboration was published in 1909. [V&A: A history of tarot cards](https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/tarot-cards)

“Correspondences” can be understood as an interpretive table through which a particular school links different symbols. Crowley's published *Liber LXXVIII*, for example, sets card names alongside Hebrew letters, zodiac signs or planets, and describes the elements and positions on the Tree of Life associated with the minor cards. It is a primary text for studying that occult tradition. It establishes that the author used those connections, not that they were objective laws present when the cards first appeared. [Crowley: Liber LXXVIII](https://sacred-texts.com/oto/lib78.htm)

Even different periods of one author's work should not be conflated. The modern editor of Mathers's 1888 *The Tarot* explicitly states that it uses Lévi's order and correspondences, rather than the Golden Dawn's later tarot teachings. Combining everything under the same author's name into an eternal standard erases the development of ideas. [Mathers: editorial note to The Tarot](https://hermeticgoldendawn.org/the-tarot/)

sources.label: V&A: A history of tarot cards
Crowley: Liber LXXVIII
Mathers: editorial note to The Tarot

sections.title: Later practitioners did not converge on one deck
sections.bodyMarkdown:
RWS brought many everyday actions into the experience of reading cards. Later, the Thoth collaboration between Crowley and Frieda Harris developed another visual language; the Warburg's exhibition material dates the related work to 1937–1943. The two decks can be compared, but every interpretation of an image in one cannot simply be transferred to the other. [The Warburg: conversation with the exhibition's co-curator](https://warburg.sas.ac.uk/news-events/blogs/tarot-origins-afterlives-conversation-director-co-curator-bill-sherman)

Another path centres on contemplation and practice. The official introduction to B.O.T.A., founded by Paul Foster Case, includes tarot meditation and the Tree of Life in its teaching. This is the organisation's account of its own tradition and should be understood as a statement of belief and practice. [B.O.T.A.: The Open Door](https://www.bota.org/membership/free-brochure-the-open-door)

The diversity of modern tarot is therefore not simply an original set of answers copied increasingly badly. Different authors, artists and groups have their own questions and deliberately revise imagery and uses. Understanding that makes it less necessary to smooth away differences when reading different guidebooks.

sources.label: The Warburg: conversation with the exhibition's co-curator
B.O.T.A.: The Open Door

sections.title: Tell the legends, but keep the question marks
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Was the Popess a particular historical person? Does tarot conceal heretical ideas? Such questions are engaging, but an evocative subject is not an established origin. Gertrude Moakley, for example, linked the Visconti-Sforza Popess with Maifreda. An article devoted to that view should likewise be read as an approach to identifying an image, not proof that all tarot came from one secret group. [Le Tarot: the Popess Maifreda](https://letarot.it/it/la-papessa-maifreda)

When you next encounter a compelling story, try a small exercise: write down separately “when this object appeared”, “who proposed this interpretation” and “what evidence connects the two”. Leave any unfilled boxes blank. Keeping the unknowns does not weaken a story; it lets readers enjoy imagination and investigation together while seeing more clearly whether they are reading history, tradition or legend.

sources.label: Le Tarot: the Popess Maifreda
